newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia starts work to mend black-white relations.
newsitem.headline: Australia starts work to mend black-white relations.

text.p: Australia officially starts work on Monday to repair divisions in society at a landmark conference called to discuss strained relations with Aborigines.

About 1,800 Aboriginal, political, business and community delegates will sit down together in Melbourne at this week's Australian Reconciliation Convention, to try to reach a common view on issues that have plagued relations for up to 200 years.

Held to coincide with the 30th anniversary of Aborigines winning the right to vote, the convention will deal with issues such as protection of Aboriginal culture and indigenous rights at a time when they are seen by some to be under attack.
Organisers hope the convention's work will culminate in 2001 with a legal pact or treaty, ensuring basic agreements reached this week are respected and guarded.

"The nation has to figure out its future -- its future in terms of a reconciled Australia, one in which it heals the wounds of the past," said Pat Dodson, chairman of the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation.
The 25-member council, an official think tank, called the three-day convention to help it fulfill its duty to produce a "national agreement of reconcilation" by the end of the century.
But the convention comes at a time of loud discord over Aboriginal issues, with farmers calling for indigenous land title to be curtailed and the country's race row still raging.
The council has warned bluntly that these two issues are undermining its work.
"The reconciliation process is at risk," council deputy chairman Ian Viner, a former Aboriginal affairs minister, said.
Race row politician Pauline Hanson, whose One Nation party urges cuts to Aboriginal welfare, will not attend the convention. "She has not registered," an organiser told Reuters on Sunday.

Prime Minister John Howard has registered to attend, despite growing criticism from Aboriginal leaders that for too long he allowed Hanson's views to go unchallenged. Aborigines also accuse him of siding with the farmers on the issue of land.

Howard will address the convention's opening ceremony on Monday, and his speech may touch another old social wound -- Australia's former policy of taking Aboriginal babies from their parents and assimilating them into the white community.
The convention is expected to coincide with the release this week of a major human rights report into the practice.
Tens of thousands of Aborigines, dubbed the "Stolen Generation", were taken from their mothers from the 1880s to the 1960s. They now demand an apology from Howard and compensation.
One delegate who will attend the convention is elderly Aboriginal activist Faith Bandler, who 30 years ago celebrated a hard-fought campaign to win Aborigines the vote.
Bandler, an early campaigner for Aborigines to be granted full citizenship in their own country, was instrumental in the holding of the referendum on May 27, 1967 which brought this about.
Bandler believes a reconciliation treaty, preferably written into the nation's constitution, would be a major step to rival the 1967 referendum. But she is not optimistic it will happen.
"This would be the second major step, but it's a little harder now than it was then," she told Reuters.
"We didn't have organised racism then. We had indifference, but there was plenty of sympathy out there and many people felt it was time for a new deal for Aborigines.
"There's some of that now and we have to find it, but it's a harder track now."
